title: The 2006–09 Mitsubishi Raider Proves History Repeats Itself

body_markdown:
To say Mitsubishi Motors has a “rocky” relationship with the American consumer might be inappropriate, as that word is[better associated](https://www.hagerty.com/media/maintenance-and-tech/what-its-like-to-own-a-unicorn-car-built-with-unobtainium-parts/) with the troubled Daihatsu brand. But the massive Japanese conglomerate still has a bumpy road in America, to the point it played charades (sorry) with customers trying to figure out the dodgy origin of their first midsize truck. Only true students of automobile history remember the 2006–09 Mitsubishi Raider, much less its connection to Dodge’s Dakota. Now this forgotten slice of history is repeating itself, because a new midsize truck from a different Mitsubishi partner[is coming soon](https://www.hagerty.com/media/news/new-mitsubishi-models-pickup-launch-date/#:~:text=Moving%20to%20the%20top%2C%20the%20truck%20on%20the%20left%20side%20is%20a%20new%20pickup%20that%20will%20be%20based%20on%20the%20Nissan%20Frontier%20and%20return%20Mitsubishi%20to%20the%20pickup%20segment%20after%20a%20long%20hiatus.) . While we wait, let’s turn back the clock a full 20 years and see how Mitsubishi got truckin’ in the 2000s.


This isn’t a particularly happy story, as the Raider’s four-year run was nothing like the memorable Mighty Max truck before it. That Mitsubishi was a compact truck, with the unique ability to help Chrysler reach that popular segment with its Ram 50 and Plymouth Arrow nameplates. Instead, the Raider a was big and brawny American, capitalizing on the growing midsize trend founded by its Dodge Dakota blueprint. The tables turned, and the market quickly determined neither Mitsubishi nor Dodge was the winner. Both rigs lacked the popular appeal of Toyota’s all-new Tacoma midsizer by a wide sales margin.


Mitsubishi


Mitsubishi


Dodge


Dodge


But Mitsubishi’s Raider wasn’t an obvious badge swap like the Ram 50 or Precis (née Hyundai Excel) before it. It possessed slicker fascias and a less utilitarian dashboard than a Dakota. There was no downside to jumping nameplates, because Chrysler’s 4.7-liter PowerTech V-8 engine was also available. Put another way, if you wanted a Dodge in a power suit, Mitsubishi ensured you lost nothing in the dressing room.


It’s fair to consider the Raider as the right truck for the Mitsubishi brand. The company likely lacked the funding to make it more unique, and the market was rapidly changing from the Mighty Max era. This is mostly because larger rigs were[more palatable](https://www.hagerty.com/media/opinion/how-regulations-made-the-small-pickup-segment-a-dinosaur-park/#newsletter-submitted:~:text=One%20answer%3A%20the%20corporate%20average%20fuel%20economy%20(CAFE)%20standard.%20It%20has%20several%20inputs%20to%20its%20complex%20calculation%2C%20including%20sales%20of%20a%20particular%20model%20as%20well%20as%20the%20model%E2%80%99s%20footprint.) to CAFE standards. But bigger trucks also provided four conventional doors as an option,[which became the rage](https://www.hagerty.com/media/car-profiles/the-1997-04-ford-f-150-legitimized-the-white-collar-truck/) , thanks to a combination of utility and family-sized practicality. The optional V-8 put the Raider in a right-sized place, smaller than a full-size truck and with performance that would make a higher-revving V-6 Tacoma struggle to keep pace.


Mitsubishi


Mitsubishi


Mitsubishi


But the appealing hardware wasn’t moving Mitsubishi’s metal, as its highest sales were a paltry 8262 units in its sophomore (2007) year. By 2009, the Raider sold fewer than 2000 units, but perhaps its badge-engineered simplicity was worthy of production for the Dakota’s entire run. It really should have existed until the 2011 model year, as the Raider wasn’t unique like a Lincoln Blackwood. It was closer to a GMC Sierra, and the Mitsubishi-Chrysler partnership remained in management’s good graces after Daimler sold Chrysler to[Cerberus Capital Management](https://www.hagerty.com/media/automotive-history/when-chrysler-tapped-mitsubishi-to-build-a-sporty-coupe-for-the-fourth-time/#:~:text=DaimlerChrysler%E2%80%99s%20dissolution%20in%202007%20led%20to%20Chrysler%20being%20sold%20to%20private%20equity%20firm%20Cerberus%20Capital%20Management%2C) . But[Fiat](https://www.reuters.com/article/world/chrysler-hyundai-mitsubishi-end-engine-tie-up-idUSTRE5894U3/) swooped in after Chrysler’s bankruptcy and made it crystal clear it wanted nothing of the relationship.


Mitsubishi likely still wanted a truck for the American market, but shopping for something is impossible when every store is closed. Suzuki had already tapped the Tennessee-made Nissan Frontier for its 2009–12 Equator pickup. Toyota and Honda rarely engage in such handshakes, and getting Ford or GM on its side would likely involve moving heaven and earth. Simply put, there was no other American-made (to skirt the[chicken tax](https://www.hagerty.com/media/automotive-history/so-what-is-the-chicken-tax-anyway/) ) truck available to the Mitsubishi brand after the 2009 model year. But before we fast forward to the latest news, let’s see what Mitsubishi actually gave the market back then.


I reviewed the V-6 Dakota with a six-speed manual back in 2009 and found little appealing—aside from the hydroformed frame’s taut dynamics—over its competition. But these days I long for the mechanical and electronic simplicity of this modest pickup, because it was an admirable performer without unnecessary turbocharging, direct injecting, and computer controlling. And buying a V-8 Raider with Mitsubishi-levels of dealership discounts would absolutely change my tune. Mitsubishi is generally regarded as a value brand in the U.S., so a cheap V-8 crew cab pickup has merit in my book.


Luckily *Motorweek* didn’t share my concerns, as their double cab Raider came with the PowerTech V-8. The 9-second run to 60 mph was nothing to write home about, but it was light years ahead of the V-6 I sampled. We both praised this platform’s handling and ride, and they got a lucky break with the Raider’s slicker, less architectural dashboard design. It’s respectable, but a far cry from a modern truck’s ability to downright eliminate noise, vibration, and harshness in an opulent cabin worthy of a Cadillac. But that “cheapness” makes the Raider more honest in our modern times.


Which I think bears repeating: This *honest* , right-sized truck was somewhat affordable, had respectable performance, plenty of visibility, and none of the cost, complexity, and cumbersome bulk of a modern truck. I hate to say it, but I’d give a lot to get back to that era of truck design. I’d even embrace the hard plastics of the period and the modest performance numbers, if only to never hear about the Audi-levels of complexity in a modern pickup ever again.


It’s hard to believe we are revisiting Mitsubishi’s Raider a full 20 years later, but a vehicle doomed to obscurity has unexpectedly become the template for Mitsubishi’s future. Thanks to its participation in the Renault-Nissan-Mitsubishi Alliance, this yet-to-be-named Mitsubishi truck will be derived from the Nissan Frontier. We[reviewed](https://www.hagerty.com/media/new-car-reviews/first-drive-2025-nissan-frontier-pro-4x-review/) the new Frontier and its minimalist VQ38 V-6 powertrain and came to the conclusion it has a “less tech-driven approach” and is a fantastic value to boot.


Mitsubishi


Mitsubishi


Nissan/Bradley Mansour


While Mitsubishi’s forthcoming lineup promises a bent toward trucks and SUVs, it is heavily camouflaged at the moment. We’ve seen the Eclipse Sportback reviews elsewhere, and it looks significantly cooler than its Nissan Leaf brother. And it has a better basic (5 years/60,000 miles vs. 3/36) and powertrain (10 years/100,000 miles vs. 5/60) warranty to lure you into a Mitsubishi dealership. Imagine such a generous warranty on a modern pickup!


The mind need not brainstorm for long, because 20 years ago we learned the Raider had all the goodness of a Dodge Dakota with that very same warranty. Mitsubishi knew what it was up against, and that warranty was a heckuva lot better than the Dakota’s (3 years/36,000 basic, 7/70 powertrain) protection plan. Combine the extra warranty with a subjectively superior interior and exterior design, and the Raider made a convincing case for itself.


So, if history is repeating, get ready to seek out a Mitsubishi dealership. They are likely to give all the merits of a naturally aspirated V-6 truck with even more (factory to dealer) discounts and deeper warranties than anyone else.


But value isn’t the only play, because this time you might actually want a basic Mitsubishi more than a mandatory turbocharged, sometimes hybrid-ized Toyota Tacoma. The once unassailable Toyota brand is getting a bit tarnished these days, so let’s ask ourselves two questions:


*Could we get this lucky again? And will we take advantage of Mitsubishi’s generosity this time?*
